intro.text: The Berlin Defence is Black's most solid answer to the Ruy Lopez and a favourite of world champions. White chooses between the forcing main line, where queens often come off early, and calmer protecting setups that keep the pieces on the board.

Black develops the king's knight and attacks White's centre pawn at once instead of first questioning the bishop. It is one of the most solid defences at the top level and leads to very different games depending on how White protects the centre.

White protects the centre pawn with a pawn and avoids the forcing endgame lines. The game stays complex with all pieces on the board; White aims for a slow build-up and a later central break, Black for active bishops and a solid centre.

Black simply takes the centre pawn after White castles. White regains it by force, and the play splits into the queenless Berlin endgame and the rook-lift lines where White pressures Black's uncastled king along the open file.

white.text: White's wins here mostly came through the queenless endgame: Bxc6 and the queen trade Qxd8 lead to positions where White develops with Nc3 and h3, puts a rook on Rd1 and brings the knight to Ne4 to press with the healthy kingside majority.

black.text: Black's winners completed development quickly with the bishop on Be6, contesting the light squares and connecting the rooks.

intro.text: Against the quiet protecting move Black develops the dark-squared bishop to its most active diagonal at once. This is the modern main reply at the top level: Black aims the bishop at White's kingside and keeps the option of supporting the centre with a pawn later.

Black protects the centre pawn with a pawn first and keeps a compact, very solid position. Play is slow; Black often fianchettoes or develops the bishop modestly and waits for White to commit before choosing a plan.
Black re-routes the knight towards the kingside so that the c-pawn can support a later central advance. It is solid but slow, and White simply develops.

white.text: White's winners kept the bishop with Ba4, developed with Nc3 and Be3, and used the jump Ng5 to probe Black's kingside.

intro.text: Black develops the dark-squared bishop actively and leaves the centre pawn to its fate for the moment. White can grab space in the centre with tempo.
Black protects the centre pawn with a pawn; solid but passive, it gives White a free hand to build the ideal centre.

Instead of the main pawn move White attacks the knight with the rook at once. Black retreats to a square that questions the bishop, and play heads for an open centre where White regains the pawn but Black's position is very solid.

The main line: White strikes in the centre to regain the pawn with interest. Black's knight retreats to hit the bishop, and the game usually goes into the famous queenless Berlin endgame or into lines where White keeps the queens.

white.text: In the endgame lines White's winning plan is the kingside majority: f4 and g4 push forward to create a passed pawn, with a knight on Ne4 or Nh4 supporting the advance.

black.text: Black's winners built a solid shelter with b6 and played h6 to keep White's pieces away from the kingside, then used the bishop pair once lines opened.

intro.text: White gives up the Spanish bishop at once to double Black's pawns, hoping to win the centre pawn or reach a slightly better structure. Black gets the bishop pair and open lines for the pieces in return.

black.text: Black's winners often castled long with O-O-O and used the kingside pawns, starting with g6, to attack White's castled king.

intro.text: White prepares a central pawn advance and makes a retreat square for the bishop. Black usually castles quickly; the position stays rich and slow, like a closed Italian game with the bishop on the long queenside diagonal.
White castles and keeps a flexible setup. Black can choose between a kingside fianchetto, a modest bishop and an early queenside expansion; both sides manoeuvre before any central break.

black.text: Black's winners rerouted the knight with Ne7 towards the kingside, contested the light squares with Be6 and struck at White's centre with the f-pawn advance f5.

intro.text: Black's knight retreats instead of taking more material, inviting White to exchange on the queenside and open the centre. Most games lead to the famous queenless endgame where structure matters more than attack.

black.text: Black's winners built the classic Berlin endgame setup with b6, securing the king's shelter on the queenside and preparing to use the bishop pair.

intro.text: Black castles and accepts that White may expand in the centre. A common idea is to meet White's central push with a timely bishop retreat and a counter-strike against White's centre.

White takes back the centre pawn with the knight, opening the e-file against Black's uncastled king. Black must untangle carefully; the usual plan is to develop the bishop to block the file and castle.
White advances in the centre with tempo instead of exchanging on the queenside. Black's knights have to find new squares and Black usually returns material to complete development.

white.text: White's winners gained queenside space with a5 and b4, lifted the rook with Ra3 to swing it across, and supported the centre pawn with Re1, c3 and sometimes f3 after Nd2.

black.text: Black's winners developed with Be6 and Bd6, challenged the queenside with b6 and placed a knight on Ne5 once White's centre pawn had gone.

intro.text: White exchanges the bishop before regaining the pawn. After Black recaptures towards the centre, White takes back material and the queens usually come off, leading to the classical Berlin endgame structure.

white.text: White's winning plan in this endgame is the kingside majority: the f-pawn advance f4 starts the march towards a passed pawn.

black.text: Black's winners tucked the king away with Kc8 and gained queenside space with a5; when the queenside was settled, the king sometimes went the other way with Ke7 to blockade White's majority.

intro.text: Both sides have castled. White prepares a slow central build-up with the queen's knight and rook, Black keeps the bishop active and prepares a pawn break in the centre or on the queenside.

white.text: White's winners kept the Spanish bishop by retreating it to Bc2, where it supports the centre and aims at Black's king.

intro.text: White develops the queen's knight towards the queenside before castling, keeping options to reroute it and to castle on either side. Black's bishop pair and open lines compensate for the damaged pawns.

white.text: White's winners used the jump Ng5 to pressure Black's kingside before Black had organised it.

black.text: Black's winners castled long with O-O-O and used queenside space with b5, using the bishop pair against White's king.

intro.text: White castles and plans to target Black's doubled pawns in a slow game. Black usually protects the centre pawn with the knight or queen and uses the bishop pair actively.

black.text: Black's winning recipe is a direct attack: the bishop pins the knight and stays on Bh5, Black castles long with O-O-O, the queen comes to Qe7 and the kingside pawns storm with h6 and g5 against White's castled king.

intro.text: White keeps the light-squared bishop instead of exchanging it, accepting a slower development to keep more tension.

white.text: White's winners developed rapidly with Qd3 and Bg5, using the lead in development against Black's uncastled king.

intro.text: Black blocks the open file with the bishop and prepares to castle. White retreats the bishop to keep it, and the game becomes an open, symmetrical position where White's lead in development is small but lasting.
Black supports the centre with a pawn, creating a solid classical structure. Typical plans are a queenside pawn expansion for Black and a slow central build-up for White.

black.text: Black's winners expanded on the queenside with a6 and b5 and rerouted the knight to Nf4, a strong square in front of White's king.

intro.text: Black exchanges knights to relieve the pressure along the open file. After White recaptures with the rook, Black castles and the position is nearly symmetrical; White plays for a small lasting edge.

white.text: White's winners developed the knight with Nc3 and jumped it to Nd5, where it presses on Black's bishop and the dark squares.

intro.text: Black returns the knight to the centre instead of retreating it to the edge. The position becomes concrete: White regains material and Black's pieces must coordinate quickly.
Black's knight takes the best square, and White now trades queens. This is the famous Berlin endgame: Black has lost the right to castle but has the bishop pair and a fortress-like structure.

white.text: White's winners pushed the kingside majority with f4, aiming for a passed pawn while Black's king is far away.

black.text: Black's winners walked the king to safety with Kc8 and Kb7 and gained queenside space with a4, fixing White's queenside pawns.

intro.text: The Berlin endgame: queens are off and Black's king has lost the right to castle, but Black has the bishop pair and a very solid position. White plays for the healthy kingside pawn majority; Black for activity of the bishops and patient defence.

black.text: Black's winners walked the king to Kc8 and Kb7, gained space with b5 or a4 and only then used the bishop pair to open lines.

intro.text: Black strikes in the centre with a pawn to open the bishop's diagonal. The pawn structure becomes unbalanced and both sides have clear targets.
Black exchanges knights to simplify. White regains the knight with the queen and keeps central space; Black must develop the bishops quickly.

White grabs central space with a pawn. Black's usual answer is to develop the bishop to the long diagonal, hitting the rook and the centre; the structure is symmetrical and play is about piece activity.

white.text: White's winners developed with Nc3 and jumped into Nd5, the key square in this symmetrical structure.

intro.text: White develops the queen's knight before committing the centre pawn, keeping flexible options for the bishop and the d-pawn.

white.text: White's winners gained queenside space with a4 and kept the bishop flexible on Bd3.

intro.text: White's main move in the Berlin endgame: it takes a square away from Black's bishop and knight and prepares kingside expansion. Black usually tucks the king away on the queenside and connects the rooks.

white.text: White's winning plan is the kingside majority: the f-pawn advance f4, prepared by the knight on Ne4 or Nc3, creates a passed pawn.

black.text: Black's winners played b6 with the king to Kc8 and Kb7, gained queenside space with a5 and a4, and rerouted the knight with Ne7 when White's kingside pawns advanced.

intro.text: Black's bishop develops actively, attacking White's rook and eyeing the centre. White retreats the rook, and the symmetrical structure gives a long technical game.

white.text: White's winners developed with Nc3, jumped into Nd5 to exchange or harass Black's bishop, and pinned with Bg5.

intro.text: A typical setup in the Berlin endgame where Black develops the light-squared bishop and brings the king towards the queenside. White tries to use space and the extra kingside pawn; Black aims to neutralise and later use the bishops.
The rook retreats to the open file. White's small lead in development and central pawn give a slight initiative; Black aims to trade the rooks on the open file and equalise.

white.text: White's winners played Nc3 and Nd5 against Black's bishop and added Bg5 to increase pressure on the dark squares.

black.text: Black's winners played on the queenside with b6 and a5, kept the knight active and used h6 to stop White's bishop from pinning.

intro.text: Black contests the open file at once, offering to exchange rooks. Many top-level games here are long technical struggles where precision decides.

white.text: White's winners centralised with Nc3 and Nd5, pinned with Bg5 and sometimes added Qe4 or the f-pawn advance f4 for kingside pressure.

black.text: Black's winners gained queenside space with a5 and b6, supported the centre with d6 and developed with Be6.
